title: GLMZ Vertical: Architecture of Accumulation
body:
# GLMZ Vertical: Architecture of Accumulation

## Not a Wedding Cake

The first thing anyone gets wrong about GLMZ's vertical structure is that they imagine it like a wedding cake: distinct layers, each level a clean horizontal plane stacked neatly on the one below, each tier a legible ring separating one stratum of the city from the next. The analogy is wrong in every particular. The tiers of GLMZ are not a wedding cake. They are sediment. They are the geological record of a city that built upward because it ran out of ground.

The upper city exists because the lower city built it. And the lower city built it without a plan, without a single authority, without any concept that it was building an upper city at all. It was building parking. It was building storage. It was building elevated highway access for a decade when traffic engineers thought three-dimensional road networks would solve urban gridlock (they did not). It was building things on top of things because the things below were full. At some point, the built-over became livable, and then lived-in, and then neighborhoods with names, and then places that people from the level below looked up at with the specific mixture of envy and resentment that defines GLMZ's vertical politics.

## The Structure Is Not Uniform

In some parts of GLMZ, the upper tier begins at twelve meters. In some parts, it begins at forty. In the Gray Zone, the distinctions between levels are so compressed — six meters between platforms in some corridors — that the tiers are less a vertical distinction than a horizontal one, with upper and lower referring to which side of a structural support you're on. In the Central Ledger district, the upper tier is a genuine architectural achievement: a grid of elevated platforms spanning four city blocks, engineered and intentional, built specifically to support the density of financial infrastructure that the district requires.

Between these extremes is everything else: the ad hoc, the improvised, the built-over, the built-under. Floors that are ceilings. Ceilings that have become floors. Buildings that were designed for one tier and now open onto two, depending on which entrance you use. The elevator in the Compound Exchange building that Covenant occupies travels from the street-level lobby to the sixteenth floor in a building that, depending on how you count, is either ten stories or twenty-two.

## Crossing Between Tiers

There is no consistent infrastructure for moving between tiers. This is perhaps the defining physical fact of GLMZ's vertical geography: the people who built the upper city did not build access to it from below, because they were building for themselves, already up there.

What exists instead is a negotiated network of crossings: the structures that link two elevated platforms belong to whoever owns those platforms, and access is governed by whatever agreement those owners have reached. Some crossings are public — old highway ramps that became pedestrian bridges, stairwells in buildings whose owners concluded that foot traffic was worth the maintenance cost. Some crossings are private — access controlled by biometric readers, keycard systems, or simply the physical fact that the door is locked and you don't have a key.

The most interesting crossings are the diagonal ones: bridges between two elevated areas that are not at the same height, connecting a platform at eighteen meters on one side to a platform at twenty-three meters on the other. These bridges were built for reasons that no longer apply, or were built without reasons by people who wanted to be connected to somewhere and simply built toward it. They give the upper city its most distinctive characteristic: from above, it looks like a graph, not a grid. The nodes are the platforms. The edges are whatever someone found worth building between them.

## What This Means for Moving Around

Navigating vertical GLMZ is a skill that has very little overlap with navigating horizontal GLMZ. You can know the street layout of a district perfectly and arrive at the base of an elevated neighborhood with no idea how to get up to it. The crossings that locals use are not documented. They are passed down the way useful knowledge always is in GLMZ: by being shown by someone who was shown by someone else, the chain of demonstrated knowledge going back to whoever first found the gap in the railing at the Halsted Bridge overpass that drops you onto the lower access gray zone of the Circuit district's second tier in forty-five seconds instead of the forty-minute walk-around.

There are guides who know the crossings. They are expensive because the knowledge is valuable and because they have generally paid for it in ways that aren't pleasant to think about.

The city also links, in places, across its own tiers — bridges that pass over the open air between elevated sections, the famous walkway at the 35th Street platform that connects the corponation quarter to the lower Circuit without touching the ground at any point, a half-kilometer span of enclosed corridor that is technically private property but has been used by the public for so long that its owners no longer attempt to close it. These cross-tier links are often the fastest routes in the city. They are also, for obvious structural reasons, the routes most likely to be unavailable without warning.
